quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-01.prompt:
A finite group $G$ is said to have property $*$ if there exists a conjugacy class $K$ of $G$ such that $G$ is generated by the elements of $K$.

(i) If $G$ has property $*$, prove that $G/G'$ is cyclic, where $G'$ is the commutator subgroup of $G$.

(ii) Show that $G$ has property $*$ if and only if $G$ is not the set-theoretic union of its proper normal subgroups.

(iii) Suppose $G=N\times M$ where $N$ is nonabelian simple and $M$ has property $*$. Prove that $G$ has property $*$. (Hint. First show that every normal subgroup of $G$ that does not contain $N$ must be contained in $M$.)
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-01.answer: (i) All elements of $K$ have the same image in the abelian group $G/G'$, which that image generates. (ii) $\langle K\rangle$ is normal, so $G=\langle g^G\rangle$ iff $g$ lies in no proper normal subgroup. (iii) A normal $L\not\supseteq N$ has $L\cap N=1$, so $L\subseteq C_G(N)=M$; then $(n,m)$ with $n\neq1$ and $m$ in no proper normal subgroup of $M$ lies in no proper normal subgroup of $G$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-02.prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and suppose that $M$ is an ideal of $R$.

(i) If $M$ is both maximal and principal, show that there is no ideal $I$ of $R$ satisfying $M>I>M^2$, where $>$ denotes strict inclusion.

(ii) Give examples to show that neither of the two conditions on $M$ in part (i) can be removed.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-02.answer: (i) If $M=(m)$ and $M^2\subseteq I\subseteq M$, let $J=\{r:rm\in I\}\supseteq M$; then $J=R$ gives $I=M$ and $J=M$ gives $I=Mm=M^2$. (ii) Maximal, not principal: $R=F[x,y]$, $M=(x,y)$, $I=(x,y^2)$. Principal, not maximal: $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $M=(4)$, $I=(8)$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-03.prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq L\subseteq E$ be fields with $\mathbb{Q}$ the rational numbers and with $|E:L|<\infty$. Let $K$ be the subfield of $E$ consisting of all those elements of $E$ which are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, and assume that $K\cap L=\mathbb{Q}$.

(i) If $\alpha\in K$, show that its minimal polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ is irreducible over $L$ and deduce that $|\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|\le|E:L|$.

(ii) Show that $|K:\mathbb{Q}|\le|E:L|$. (Hint. Start with a subfield $M$ of $K$ maximal with the property that $|M:\mathbb{Q}|\le|E:L|$.)
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-03.answer: (i) The coefficients of a monic factor over $L$ are polynomials in roots of $f$, hence algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, and lie in $L\subseteq E$, so they lie in $K\cap L=\mathbb{Q}$; thus $|L[\alpha]:L|=\deg f\le|E:L|$. (ii) Take $M\subseteq K$ of maximal degree $\le|E:L|$; for $\alpha\in K$, $M[\alpha]=\mathbb{Q}[\gamma]$ (primitive element) has degree $\le|E:L|$ by (i), so $M[\alpha]=M$; hence $K=M$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-04.prompt:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $K$ and let $S$ and $T$ be $K$-linear operators on $V$. Suppose that $S$ is one-to-one, that $T(v)=0$ for some $0\neq v\in V$, and that $TS-ST=S$.

(i) For every integer $n\ge0$, prove that $S^n(v)$ is an eigenvector for $T$ and determine the corresponding eigenvalue.

(ii) If $K$ has characteristic $0$, prove that $\dim_K V=\infty$.

(iii) If $K$ has characteristic $p>0$, then $\dim_K V$ can be finite. Give a concrete example of such a finite-dimensional situation when $p=3$.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-04.answer: (i) $TS^n=S^nT+nS^n$, so $T(S^nv)=n\,S^nv$ with $S^nv\ne0$: eigenvalue $n$. (ii) In characteristic $0$ the eigenvalues $0,1,2,\dots$ are distinct, giving infinitely many independent vectors. (iii) $K=\mathbb{F}_3$, $V=K^3$, $S$ the cyclic shift $v_i\mapsto v_{i+1}$ (indices mod 3), $T=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,2)$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-05.prompt:
Let $q$ be a prime power and let $F$ be the finite field of size $q$. Let
$$f(x)=\frac{x^5-1}{x-1}=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1\in F[x].$$

(i) If $f(x)$ has a root in $F$, show that $f(x)$ splits completely over $F$, and prove that this happens precisely when $q\equiv0$ or $1\bmod 5$.

(ii) If $f(x)$ has an irreducible monic factor $g(x)$ of degree $2$, show that $g(x)$ has constant term equal to $1$.

(iii) Factor $f(x)$ explicitly into irreducible quadratic factors when $q=29$.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1996s-05.answer: (i) A root $\zeta\ne1$ has order 5, so $\zeta,\zeta^2,\zeta^3,\zeta^4$ are the roots; $\zeta=1$ forces characteristic 5 and $f=(x-1)^4$. Roots exist iff $5\mid q$ or $5\mid q-1$. (ii) The constant term $c$ is a product of two 5th roots of unity, so $c^5=1$ in $F$, and $F$ has no element of order 5, so $c=1$. (iii) Over $\mathbb{F}_{29}$: $f=(x^2+6x+1)(x^2-5x+1)$.
